Don't grab a new identity just to make the not-knowing stop. You can keep your routines, take care of your body, grieve, and stay with your little one while the next life takes shape.

t65y_le1p3d: And if you miss someone, the missing doesn't have to be one more problem to fix. Sometimes the ache can work like a doorbell for love. If there's love there, let "I miss you" turn into "I love you," or send a simple wish, something like "May you be safe. May you be held in love." Picture them if that helps, or just feel which way the care is going.
t65y_le1p4f: It's about what happens in you, by the way. You don't have to believe they get anything from it. It also doesn't replace grieving or calling them, and your boundaries still count. If it starts to feel compulsive, make it simpler: "I miss you, and I care." And give a little of that care to the part of you that's still here.
t65y_ks1p1d: If you might act on it soon, stop reading for a second and get another person involved, right now. A crisis line or emergency number counts. Then put some distance between you and the means. That goes for anyone who's about to act or can't stop themselves, anyone badly disoriented or high or drunk, and anyone with the means right there. Not sure which you are? Treat it as if you're about to act. None of this answers whether life is worth living. It keeps the question open long enough to look at it.
t65y_ks1p1e: First things first. If you're close to acting, get another human being involved now (a crisis line or emergency number counts), and get some distance from the means. Do this if you can't stop yourself, if you're badly disoriented or intoxicated, or if the means are in front of you, and do it if you can't tell whether you're about to act. It isn't my answer to whether life is worth living. It just buys the question enough time to be looked at.
t65y_ks1p2d: Then, before anything philosophical, check that there's an adult in the room. If the part that wants to die feels like all of you, try the noticing from Noticing Counts or the borrowed adulthood trick, and see if any part of you can watch what's happening, protect your body, or at least hold off on something that can't be undone. If none can right now, the questions below can wait. The person you reached out to is your grown-up for the moment.
t65y_ks1p2e: Is there an adult in the room? Check that before getting philosophical. When the part that wants to die feels like the whole of you, use the noticing from Noticing Counts, or borrow an adult, and invite in anything in you that can watch. A part that just wants to keep your body safe counts, and so does one that can put off a decision you can't undo. If nothing in you can watch yet, skip the questions for now and lean on the person you called.
t65y_ks1p4c: Buddhism, for what it's worth, doesn't treat death as an off switch, or as a free get-out-of-jail card back to the source. It says repeated thought and intention shape the mind, that this keeps going through death and rebirth, that hell realms are possible, and that a human birth is a rare shot at understanding suffering and ending its causes. You don't have to believe any of that.
t65y_ks1p4d: In Buddhism, death isn't an off switch. It isn't a get-out-of-jail-free card back to the source, either. What it teaches is that what you keep thinking and intending shapes your mind, that this carries on through death and rebirth (hell realms included), and that being born human is a rare chance to understand suffering and end its causes. Believing it is optional.
t65y_ks1p6c: If losing everything is already on the table, what change is still too scary to try? Maybe a relationship. Maybe a job, or where you live, or who you've always been told you are. Those changes cost something, and some can't be undone, but they're smaller than dying, and you can make them later, calmer, with help. While you still have a body and people around you, look into those questions, and into the life you've been afraid to change.
t65y_ks1p6d: So, if everything's already on the table, what's the change you still can't bring yourself to make? Leaving? Quitting? Moving? Telling your family who you really are? Those aren't free, and you can't always take them back, but they're smaller than dying, and they can wait until you're calmer and have some help. Look at that life you've been afraid to change while you still have a human body, and people around to help redirect the path.
t65y_fg1p2e: Want to know what usually helps? Seeing how their history and their pain, and what they could and couldn't do by then, shaped the thing they did. Given everything they'd become by that moment, it was the only move they had. Hurt people often pass on pain they never processed. When that's something you see yourself, nobody needs to tell you to forgive. It can happen on its own, and the rage that made them the one guilty person softens into something truer.
t65y_fg1p3ad: Seeing that doesn't make what they did harmless. It doesn't mean there was no other option in theory, either. It just means punishing them can't go back in time and hand them the awareness or support they didn't have. The useful work is repairing what you can and making a different response easier from here on. The harm is real, and accountability stays.
t65y_fg1p4d: Forgiving yourself runs the same way (and if you can't forgive yourself, forgiving them tends to get harder too). Own what you did and how it landed, and only that, not what was someone else's. Let the remorse register and fix what you can, and then you're allowed to stop punishing yourself, with the responsibility still yours. Some harms take years. Living in resentment for good is a trap too, so keep coming back to how they got capable of it, until that understanding changes how you feel.
t65y_ba1p1d: Reparenting usually sounds like something you do alone, or in a therapist's office. But your little one got hurt in relationships, so a relational injury can only heal so far in isolation. Sometimes one person ends up doing a lot of the borrowed-grown-up jobs for you: cooking, planning, doctor appointments, rides, social plans, reassurance, protection, company, or just being the competent one in the room. If you've got someone like that while you're struggling, that's a real blessing.
t65y_ba1p2d: Little by little, reparenting can help you take in what they've been showing you and practice it yourself. Some jobs can get spread around, to friends, community, professionals, routines, a good calendar. So which of those jobs can become more yours? Which are healthier shared? Which really belong in that relationship? The point is for your little one to feel cared for through more than one door, without making that relationship any less precious.
t65y_sh1d: Some people have the opposite problem: it feels like they're connecting, and it's all happening near the surface. Meditating for hours and then sleeping (especially the second sleep, after you've already slept once) can bring up much more direct stuff. If the dream that night has way more feeling and need in it than the daytime session ever got to, take that gap as a sign the session stayed shallow, a sign and not a verdict. Ask what's available now, and what you make of it. And if nightmares start wrecking your sleep, change the dose, earlier in the day or shorter, before you give up on the whole thing.
t65y_secle1p2d:
# When One Life Has Ended and the Next Hasn’t Begun

Your little one can get really loud in the gap after one life ends and before the next one has formed. A breakup will do it, or moving to another country, an illness, losing your faith or a role, your youngest moving out. So can leaving a family or community, or staying in one on new terms. Tibetan Buddhism calls an in-between state a bardo. You don't have to buy what it teaches about death and rebirth to use the everyday part: endings leave a stretch where the old you is gone and the new one hasn't shown up.

So what has really ended? And what are you still trying to keep alive? What don't you know yet, and what is your little one afraid is going to happen in the gap? A small ritual can help mark the ending without pretending you know what comes next, like boxing up their stuff or one last walk around the old neighborhood. Don't grab a new identity just to make the not-knowing stop. You can keep your routines, take care of your body, grieve, and stay with your little one while the next life takes shape.
